scan.summary: This is your own written Emergency Action Plan for the Portland warehouse, lab and offices. It covers fire, chemical release, medical emergencies and earthquake. Oregon OSHA requires a written plan because you have more than 10 employees, so this is your document to keep up to date. It already covers alarms, evacuation routes, headcounts and first aid. But it was last revised in February 2021, it leaves out several elements the Oregon rule requires, and the maps and rosters it depends on are not in the file.
scan.freshness_note: The plan was last revised in February 2021, about 5 years and 7 months ago. It says the facilities lead reviews it every January, but the file shows no review since 2021. Ask whether a newer version or signed January review records exist. If they don't, a review and update is overdue.

gaps.title: No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
gaps.description: The plan never says who calls 911 or the fire department, or how an employee raises the alarm for a fire, spill or medical emergency. It only says pull stations exist and that emergency medical services 'are called' for injuries, without saying by whom.
gaps.fix: Add a short 'Reporting an emergency' section. Cover pulling the nearest station, calling 911, who makes the call (for example, reception or the incident coordinator), and what to tell the dispatcher, such as the chemical involved and the SDS.
gaps.locator: not in the document (would fit after section 2, Alarm system)
gaps.quote: Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor first aid.

gaps.title: Shutdown of critical equipment before evacuation is not set out
gaps.description: When people evacuate, the plan tells them to secure nothing that takes more than a few seconds. It never says whether any equipment must be shut down or run in an emergency, or who does it. Examples would be lab processes, transfer pumps, forklifts or chemical dispensing. The only shutdown mentioned is the ventilation during shelter-in-place.
gaps.fix: Decide whether any equipment needs shutting down before people leave. If it does, name the equipment, the person or job title responsible, and when that person must stop and leave. If nothing needs shutting down, say so in the plan.
gaps.quote: secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds

gaps.title: No names or job titles of people to contact about the plan
gaps.description: The plan refers to a 'facilities lead' and an 'incident coordinator' but names no one. It gives no contact for employees who want more information about the plan or their duties under it. It also never says who acts as incident coordinator.
gaps.fix: Add a contacts section with the names or job titles, and phone numbers, of the incident coordinator, the facilities lead and a backup.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(f), not fully confirmed. The search confirmed paragraphs (2)(a) to (d) of the Oregon rule. The letter (f) follows the matching federal rule, 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(6), and the earlier reading.
gaps.quote: reported at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point

gaps.title: Plan does not say whether employees respond to chemical spills
gaps.description: This is a chemical distributor with a warehouse, loading dock and lab. The plan lists 'chemical release' in its scope but only covers exposure first aid and shelter-in-place for releases outside. It never says whether employees clean up small spills themselves or evacuate and call an outside hazmat team. That choice decides whether the HAZWOPER emergency response rules apply.
gaps.fix: Add a spill section. Either state that employees evacuate and outside responders handle all releases except small spills they can safely clean up, or, if employees will respond, set up an emergency response plan and training under HAZWOPER.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.120(q)(1), which Oregon OSHA adopts by reference (belief, not checked against Oregon's adoption)
gaps.locator: section 1, Purpose and scope (page 2); response procedure not in the document
gaps.quote: when there is a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility

gaps.title: Earthquake named in scope but no earthquake procedure
gaps.description: Section 1 lists earthquake as a covered emergency, but no section says what to do in one, for example drop, cover and hold on, staying away from racking, and when to evacuate afterward. Portland is in a significant earthquake zone, and the warehouse has storage racks.
gaps.fix: Add an earthquake procedure: what to do during shaking, then evacuation and headcount once shaking stops, checking for chemical spills or leaks, and staying away from damaged racking.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(a) (evacuation procedures), applied to an emergency the plan itself names. This link is inferred.
gaps.locator: section 1 names it (page 2); procedure not in the document
gaps.quote: fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency

gaps.title: Annual January review not shown
gaps.description: The plan says the facilities lead reviews it every January, but it still shows a February 2021 revision. The file holds no record of any review in 2022 through 2026.
gaps.fix: Do the review now. Update the revision date, and keep a dated, signed review log with the plan each January.
gaps.locator: section 6, Training and review (page 5); cover date (page 1)
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January

gaps.title: Appendices A and B not in the file
gaps.description: The exit-route assignments rely on the Appendix A evacuation maps. The names of the floor wardens and trained first-aid responders are only on the Appendix B roster. Neither appendix is in this file, so the plan as held is incomplete on exit routes and who has which duty.
gaps.fix: Attach the current evacuation maps and a dated warden and first-aid responder roster to the plan.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(a) (exit route assignments). The link to this rule is inferred.
gaps.locator: section 6 lists the appendices (page 5); appendix content not in the document
gaps.quote: Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)

scan.confidence_notes: All five pages are clear text, and every quote is taken from them. I'm confident about the document type, site, February 2021 revision and the facts listed. I checked the current Oregon rule text for paragraphs (2)(a) to (d) of OAR 437-002-0042, so the reporting and equipment-shutdown gaps rest on confirmed text. The paragraph letter for the contacts requirement ((2)(f)) comes from the matching federal rule and the earlier reading, not from the Oregon text itself. The HAZWOPER spill gap rests on my understanding of 29 CFR 1910.120(q) and Oregon's adoption of it, which I have not checked. The earthquake and appendix gaps are good practice, or tied to the rule by inference. Nothing here says the plan meets the rule overall. This reading found no new gaps beyond the seven already open. Sections 1, 4 and 5 appear to cover evacuation routes, headcounts, and rescue and medical duties. The monthly alarm test due date (2026-10-05) is worked out from the calendar. The January 2027 review date is inferred from 'every January'.

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)
Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)
